chapter_summary:
As your Roblox games grow more complex, you'll quickly find yourself writing similar pieces of code multiple times. This is where functions become indispensable. Functions are self-contained blocks of code designed to perform a specific task. They allow you to organize your code, make it more readable, and, most importantly, reuse logic without duplicating it. This adherence to the "Don't Repeat Yourself" (DRY) principle is a hallmark of good programming practice. Instead of writing the same 10 lines of code every time a player collects a coin, you can put those 10 lines into a function and simply "call" that function whenever a coin is collected.

Defining a function in Lua is straightforward. You use the `function` keyword, followed by the function's name, a list of parameters in parentheses, and then the `end` keyword to close the function block. For example: `function GreetPlayer(name) print("Hello, " .. name .. "!") end`. To execute the code inside a function, you simply "call" it by its name, followed by parentheses containing any required arguments: `GreetPlayer("Robloxian")`. The `name` inside the `GreetPlayer` function is a *parameter*, a placeholder for a value that will be passed into the function when it's called. The actual value passed during the call (e.g., `"Robloxian"`) is an *argument*. Functions can take zero, one, or multiple parameters, separated by commas.

Functions can also send information back to the part of the code that called them. This is done using the `return` keyword. When Lua encounters `return`, the function immediately stops executing, and the value(s) specified after `return` are sent back. For example: `function CalculateDamage(baseDamage, multiplier) return baseDamage * multiplier end`. You can then capture this returned value in a variable: `local finalDamage = CalculateDamage(20, 1.5)`. A unique and powerful feature of Lua is its ability to return *multiple values* from a single function. For instance, `function GetPlayerStats() return "Robloxian", 100, true end`. You can then capture these multiple values like this: `local name, health, isAlive = GetPlayerStats()`. This is incredibly useful for returning related pieces of information from a single operation.

Just like variables, functions also have scope. It's generally best practice to declare functions as `local` to limit their visibility and prevent naming conflicts. A local function is only accessible within the script or block where it's defined. `local function UpdateScore(points) playerScore = playerScore + points end`. If you omit `local`, the function becomes global, which can be problematic in larger games where different scripts might accidentally define functions with the same name. Global functions are sometimes used for utility functions that are truly intended to be accessible across multiple modules, but even then, careful naming and module patterns are preferred. A common mistake is defining a function globally when it's only needed internally, leading to potential clashes and making code harder to debug.

Anonymous functions, also known as unnamed functions or lambda functions, are functions without a specific name. They are often defined and used immediately, or passed as arguments to other functions. In Roblox, anonymous functions are most frequently seen when connecting to events. For example, when a player touches a part, you might want to run some code. Roblox's event system allows you to connect a function to an event: `part.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart) print(otherPart.Name .. " touched the part!") end)`. Here, the `function(otherPart) ... end` is an anonymous function that gets executed whenever the `Touched` event fires. This is a very powerful pattern for creating responsive and interactive game elements.

When designing functions, consider their purpose. A good function should ideally do one thing and do it well. Avoid creating "god functions" that try to handle too many responsibilities. This makes your code harder to read, test, and maintain. Also, ensure your function parameters are clearly named and that the function's return values are well-understood. A common mistake is to have functions that modify global state without explicitly indicating it, making it difficult to track changes. If a function modifies a global variable, it's good practice to document this behavior. Safety-wise, be mindful of recursion (a function calling itself). While powerful, infinite recursion will lead to a stack overflow error and crash your script. Always ensure recursive functions have a clear base case to stop the recursion.

```lua
-- Chapter 2.3: Functions: Reusable Code Blocks

-- 1. Defining and Calling a Local Function (Best Practice)
local function GreetPlayer(playerName)
    print("Welcome, " .. playerName .. " to our Roblox world!")
end

-- Calling the function
GreetPlayer("RobloxianBuilder")
GreetPlayer("GameDevJunior")

-- 2. Function with Parameters and a Single Return Value
local function CalculateTotalDamage(baseDamage, criticalHitMultiplier)
    local totalDamage = baseDamage * criticalHitMultiplier
    return totalDamage
end

local enemyBaseAttack = 25
local critMultiplier = 1.5
local finalAttackDamage = CalculateTotalDamage(enemyBaseAttack, critMultiplier)
print("Enemy's final attack damage: " .. finalAttackDamage)

local playerBaseDefense = 10
local damageTaken = finalAttackDamage - playerBaseDefense
if damageTaken < 0 then damageTaken = 0 end -- Ensure damage isn't negative
print("Player took " .. damageTaken .. " damage.")

-- 3. Function with Multiple Return Values
local function GetPlayerStats(playerID)
    -- In a real game, this would fetch data from a data store or player object
    if playerID == 1 then
        return "Alice", 120, true, "Warrior"
    elseif playerID == 2 then
        return "Bob", 80, false, "Mage"
    else
        return "Unknown", 0, false, "NoClass"
    end
end

local p1Name, p1Health, p1IsOnline, p1Class = GetPlayerStats(1)
print(p1Name .. " (Class: " .. p1Class .. ") - Health: " .. p1Health .. ", Online: " .. tostring(p1IsOnline))

local p2Name, p2Health, p2IsOnline, p2Class = GetPlayerStats(2)
print(p2Name .. " (Class: " .. p2Class .. ") - Health: " .. p2Health .. ", Online: " .. tostring(p2IsOnline))

-- 4. Anonymous Functions (commonly used with Roblox events)
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Size = Vector3.new(4, 1, 4)
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 0.5, 0)
part.Anchored = true
part.BrickColor = BrickColor.new("Bright green")
part.Parent = workspace
part.Name = "TouchDetector"

print("\n--- Touch Detector Setup ---")
print("Part '" .. part.Name .. "' created at " .. tostring(part.Position))

-- Connect an anonymous function to the Touched event
part.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
    local humanoid = otherPart.Parent:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if humanoid then
        local player = game.Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(otherPart.Parent)
        if player then
            print(player.Name .. " touched the TouchDetector!")
            -- Common mistake: Forgetting to check if 'player' exists before using it
            -- This function runs every time something touches the part.
            -- In a real game, you might give points, heal, or teleport the player.
        else
            print("Something without a player character touched the TouchDetector: " .. otherPart.Name)
        end
    else
        print("Non-humanoid part touched the TouchDetector: " .. otherPart.Name)
    end
end)

print("TouchDetector event connected. Try touching the green part in Workspace!")

-- Wait a bit to allow the event to be triggered in Studio
wait(10)

-- Clean up the part after demonstration
part:Destroy()
print("\nTouchDetector part destroyed.")

-- Common mistake: Forgetting 'end' for function or ')' for call.
-- function MyBadFunc(param -- Missing ')'
--   print(param)
-- end
```

screens.title: Functions: Reusable Code Blocks
screens.subtitle: Write, call, and design functions in Lua to keep your Roblox code clean and reusable.

narration.text: In this lesson we focus on functions—self-contained blocks of code that perform a single task. You'll learn why functions are the best tool for following the Don't Repeat Yourself principle and how they make game code easier to read, test, and maintain. We'll cover defining and calling functions, passing parameters and receiving return values, how Lua supports returning multiple values, and the difference between local and global scope. You'll also see how anonymous functions power event handling in Roblox, such as responding to a player touching a part. By the end you should be able to refactor repeated logic into local functions, use parameters and returns to pass data cleanly, and choose the right scope so your functions don't collide across scripts. As a concrete example, you'll see how a small function can replace repeated damage calculations when a player is hit by different enemies. One common misconception is that functions slow your game; in practice they make logic clearer and often faster to maintain. Think about a piece of repeated logic you have now—how would a function make it clearer? That question will guide your practice.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Functions let you group repeated code into named, reusable units so you write less, test more easily, and reduce bugs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Functions Overview

Functions: Reusable Code Blocks

Encapsulate logic, pass data with parameters, return results, and connect behavior to events with anonymous functions.

Why functions

Avoid repeating code like damage calculations, UI updates, or inventory checks. Functions make changes in one place.

When to use

Whenever a task is repeated, conceptually separate, or benefits from testing. Small, focused functions are easier to reason about.

Concrete example

Replace repeated lines that compute damage with a CalculateDamage function that takes base and multiplier and returns a value you can reuse across enemy types.

DRY Principle
Group repeated logic into functions to avoid duplication and reduce bugs.
Scope Safety

Returns

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will define and call functions in Lua, pass data to them using parameters, and capture their return values. You will learn to prefer local functions for scope safety and understand when a global function might be appropriate. You'll also practice returning multiple values from a single function, which is a Lua-specific feature that simplifies returning related data. Lastly, you'll use anonymous functions to respond to events in Roblox, such as a part being touched. Each objective combines definition, a short example, and why the skill matters. For instance, being able to return multiple values makes it simple to get a player's name and health in a single call without extra table unpacking. Understanding local scope prevents accidental overwrites when many scripts run concurrently. As you practice, aim to write small functions that do one thing well and to document when a function changes global state. These habits will make your code easier to debug and safer to reuse.

screens.title: What is a function?
screens.subtitle: Definition, purpose, and the DRY principle

narration.text: A function is a named, self-contained block of code that performs a single task and can be invoked from other places in your script. Functions let you encapsulate behavior—such as calculating damage, updating a score, or spawning an item—so that the same logic doesn't have to be rewritten. The central programming idea behind functions is the Don't Repeat Yourself principle. For example, instead of writing the same ten lines that award a coin many times, you write a GiveCoin function that accepts a player and coin value and call it whenever a coin is collected. This makes maintenance much easier: change the logic once in the function and every call benefits. A common misconception is that functions are only for big features. In reality, small functions with a single responsibility are far more useful because they are easier to test and combine. As a quick check, ask whether a block of code can be described as one clear action—if so, it probably belongs in a function. Try to keep functions focused: splitting complex tasks into helper functions prevents "god functions" that are hard to debug.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A function groups code into a reusable unit to do one task well, following the DRY principle.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › What is a function?
Core concept

Function — reusable block

A function encapsulates a single task so it can be called many times without copying code. This reduces bugs and centralizes changes.

Metaphor
Think of a function like a vending machine: you provide input, it performs a job, and you get a predictable result.
Common mistake
Making god functions that do too much. Prefer many small functions instead of one large one doing unrelated tasks.
Example
Replace repeated coin-award lines with a function like GiveCoin(player, value) so you change the logic in one place.
Key Takeaway

Group repeated behavior into named functions that do a single job; this simplifies testing and reuse.

Check your understanding
  • Can you name one repeated block in your project that could be a function?
  • Is that block doing only one clear job?

screens.title: Defining and calling functions in Lua
screens.subtitle: Syntax, parameters, and the difference between parameters and arguments

narration.text: Defining a function in Lua uses the function keyword followed by a name, parameter list, body, and end. A parameter is a placeholder inside the function definition; an argument is the actual value you pass when calling it. For example, a greeting function takes a name parameter and prints a message when called with a player name. It's important to name parameters clearly so callers know what to pass. When you call a function, you use parentheses and provide arguments in the same order as parameters. Functions can have zero or many parameters separated by commas. One common error is mismatching the number of parameters and the arguments you expect; Lua will not throw a compile error but the behavior may be unexpected. Another best practice is to keep side effects explicit: prefer functions that return results rather than always printing or changing global state. In the code panel you can see an example of a local greeting function and two calls demonstrating different arguments. Practice reading code from the caller's perspective: what values flow into the function and what does it produce?

keyIdea.title: Syntax tip
keyIdea.text: Parameters are variables in the definition; arguments are the actual values you pass when calling the function.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Defining & calling
Code Example
-- Define a local function
local function GreetPlayer(name)
  print("Welcome, " .. name .. " to our Roblox world!")
end

-- Call the function with different arguments
GreetPlayer("RobloxianBuilder")
GreetPlayer("GameDevJunior")
This example shows a local function named GreetPlayer with a single parameter. The calls pass different arguments to change the output.
Key points
  • Use local function to limit scope unless you intentionally need a global.
  • Choose descriptive parameter names so the purpose is obvious to callers.
  • Lua doesn't require type declarations—document expected types in comments or names.
Common misconception
Missing or mismatched parameters won't always raise a clear error. Verify the values you pass and use checks when needed.
Check your understanding

Try renaming the parameter to playerName and call the function with a simulated player string to see the output change.

screens.title: Return values and capturing results
screens.subtitle: Use return to send results back to the caller and store them in variables

narration.text: Functions often produce values you need to use elsewhere. In Lua, the return keyword immediately stops the function and sends the specified value back to the caller. You capture that value by assigning the function call to a variable. For example, a CalculateTotalDamage function can accept a base damage and multiplier, return the computed value, and let the caller decide what to do with it. This separation keeps calculation pure and side effects under control. Always think about whether a function should print or perform changes, or should simply return data for the caller to act on. A common pitfall is relying on implicit global changes instead of returning values; that can create hidden dependencies and make testing harder. The code panel demonstrates computing damage, capturing the returned value, and ensuring negative damage won't be applied by clamping to zero. Practice writing functions that return values for the caller to evaluate; this pattern scales cleanly when composing functions. Return values and capturing results means use return to pass results back and keep functions focused on producing values rather than causing many side effects.. In practical terms, use return to send results back to the caller and store them in variables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Return pattern
keyIdea.text: Use return to pass results back and keep functions focused on producing values rather than causing many side effects.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Return values
Code Walkthrough
local function CalculateTotalDamage(baseDamage, criticalHitMultiplier)
  local totalDamage = baseDamage * criticalHitMultiplier
  return totalDamage
end

local enemyBaseAttack = 25
local critMultiplier = 1.5
local finalAttackDamage = CalculateTotalDamage(enemyBaseAttack, critMultiplier)
print("Enemy's final attack damage: " .. finalAttackDamage)

local playerBaseDefense = 10
local damageTaken = finalAttackDamage - playerBaseDefense
if damageTaken < 0 then damageTaken = 0 end
print("Player took " .. damageTaken .. " damage.")
The function calculates a number and returns it. The caller stores it in finalAttackDamage and uses it in later logic, keeping calculation and decision separate.
Why it matters

Returning values makes functions composable and testable. You can change how results are consumed without changing the function internals.

Pitfall

Functions that both return values and silently mutate many globals are harder to reason about. Prefer one clear behavior.

Key Takeaway

Return computed values and let the caller perform side effects like printing or applying damage.

screens.title: Multiple return values in Lua
screens.subtitle: Return several related pieces of information from one function

narration.text: Lua supports returning multiple values from a single function call, which simplifies functions that naturally produce several results. For example, a GetPlayerStats function might return a player's name, health, online status, and class in one call. You capture these values by listing multiple variables on the left-hand side of an assignment. This avoids packing and unpacking tables when you only need a few simple values. One useful pattern is returning a primary result plus metadata or a success flag, such as returning a position and a boolean that indicates whether the position is valid. A common misconception is that multiple returns are less clear than returning a table. Use multiple returns when the values are few and naturally ordered; prefer descriptive tables when named fields improve readability. The code panel shows a GetPlayerStats example and how to capture its multiple returns. Practice by writing functions that return both a result and a status flag to make error handling explicit. Multiple return values in Lua means return many simple, related values directly when order is logical; use tables when named fields improve clarity.. In practical terms, return several related pieces of information from one function. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Multiple returns
keyIdea.text: Return many simple, related values directly when order is logical; use tables when named fields improve clarity.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Multiple returns
Code Example
local function GetPlayerStats(playerID)
  if playerID == 1 then
    return "Alice", 120, true, "Warrior"
  elseif playerID == 2 then
    return "Bob", 80, false, "Mage"
  else
    return "Unknown", 0, false, "NoClass"
  end
end

local p1Name, p1Health, p1IsOnline, p1Class = GetPlayerStats(1)
print(p1Name .. " (Class: " .. p1Class .. ") - Health: " .. p1Health .. ", Online: " .. tostring(p1IsOnline))
Capture values in order. Use clear variable names that match the returned values to avoid confusion about which value is which.
Best practice

When returning multiple values, document their order in comments or in the function name so callers know what to expect.

When not to use

If a function returns many unrelated values or more than a handful, prefer returning a table with named fields for clarity.

Quick exercise

Write a function that returns x, y, z coordinates and a boolean indicating validity. Capture them into four variables and print the validity state.

screens.title: Local vs Global functions
screens.subtitle: Scope, safety, and when to avoid globals

narration.text: Function scope determines where a function can be accessed. A local function is declared with the local keyword and is visible only in the script or block where it is defined. This is the preferred pattern in Roblox because it prevents naming collisions between scripts and keeps behavior encapsulated. A global function, declared without local, is visible to any script that runs in the same environment. Globals can be useful for intentional utilities, but they introduce risk: two scripts might accidentally define the same global name and overwrite one another, causing silent bugs. Local functions also have a mild performance benefit because local lookups are faster than global table lookups. A frequent mistake is defining a function globally when it is only used internally. If you need cross-script access, consider using ModuleScripts that explicitly return functions instead of polluting the global environment. When deciding, ask whether the function truly needs to be called by multiple unrelated scripts. If not, prefer local. Local vs Global functions means prefer local functions for safety; use globals only when a function is intentionally shared across scripts and documented.. In practical terms, scope, safety, and when to avoid globals. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Scope rule
keyIdea.text: Prefer local functions for safety; use globals only when a function is intentionally shared across scripts and documented.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Local vs Global
Local Function
Declared with local, accessible only inside the defining script or block. Limits accidental overwrites and supports encapsulation.
local function UpdateScore(points)
  playerScore = playerScore + points
end
Global Function
No local keyword means other scripts can access it. Risky if not intentionally shared because of silent overwrites.
function UpdateScore(points)
  playerScore = playerScore + points
end
Common problem

Two scripts defining the same global function name can silently overwrite behavior. Prefer ModuleScripts or local functions instead.

screens.title: Anonymous functions and events
screens.subtitle: Use unnamed functions with :Connect to respond to gameplay events

narration.text: Anonymous functions are unnamed functions often used for short, inline callbacks. In Roblox, events like part. Touched call for a small function to run when the event fires. You typically pass an anonymous function directly to the Connect method, and it receives event-specific arguments such as the otherPart that touched a part. This keeps the event logic near the connection, improving readability. When writing event callbacks, always validate the inputs: check whether the touching object has a Humanoid or whether GetPlayerFromCharacter returns a valid player before using it. Another misconception is that anonymous functions must be short; if the logic grows, extract it into a named local function and call it from the anonymous wrapper. The code example creates a Part, connects an anonymous function to its Touched event, checks for a humanoid, and safely handles both player and non-player touches. Practice by adding a small reward only when a player touches a part and guard against nil values to avoid runtime errors. Anonymous functions and events means use anonymous functions for concise event callbacks, and validate event arguments to avoid errors when non-player objects trigger the event.. In practical terms, use unnamed functions with :connect to respond to gameplay events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Event pattern
keyIdea.text: Use anonymous functions for concise event callbacks, and validate event arguments to avoid errors when non-player objects trigger the event.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Anonymous functions
Event code
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Size = Vector3.new(4, 1, 4)
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 0.5, 0)
part.Anchored = true
part.BrickColor = BrickColor.new("Bright green")
part.Parent = workspace
part.Name = "TouchDetector"

part.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
  local humanoid = otherPart.Parent:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
  if humanoid then
    local player = game.Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(otherPart.Parent)
    if player then
      print(player.Name .. " touched the TouchDetector!")
    else
      print("Non-player character touched the part: " .. otherPart.Name)
    end
  else
    print("Non-humanoid part touched the TouchDetector: " .. otherPart.Name)
  end
end)
Validate everything in the callback. Anonymous functions are great for short handlers; extract logic if the handler becomes long.
Practical advice

Guard the callback so a non-player object doesn't cause runtime errors. Check player existence before using player properties.

Gotcha

Forgetting to check for a player or humanoid will cause nil index errors when the event fires with unexpected parts.

Key Takeaway

Use anonymous functions for event callbacks, but validate inputs and extract to named functions if logic grows.

screens.title: Designing good functions
screens.subtitle: Single responsibility, clear parameters, and documenting side effects

narration.text: Designing functions well means keeping them small, focused, and predictable. Aim for single responsibility: a function should do one thing and do it well, such as calculating a value or validating input, but not both at once. Name parameters to reveal their expected type or meaning, for example playerName or baseDamage. Document any function that changes global state so callers know the side effects. Another practical rule is to prefer returning values rather than printing or mutating globals within the function; this separation makes composition and unit testing easier. When functions must modify global variables, add explicit comments and consider moving shared behavior to ModuleScripts so the relationship is clear. Also be mindful of recursion: if you write a recursive function, ensure there is a base case to stop the calls, otherwise you risk a stack overflow. A common pitfall is verbose functions that mix UI updates with core logic. Break those apart into pure logic functions and thin wrappers that perform display updates. Designing good functions means write small, well-named functions that do one thing; document when they modify global state and avoid mixing logic with ui work.. In practical terms, single responsibility, clear parameters, and documenting side effects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Design rule
keyIdea.text: Write small, well-named functions that do one thing; document when they modify global state and avoid mixing logic with UI work.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Designing functions
Process Checklist
  1. Does the function do one clear task? If not, split it.
  2. Are parameters named to reveal expected data?
  3. Does it return values instead of mutating globals where possible?
  4. Is any global modification documented and intentional?
  5. For recursion, is there a clear base case to stop calls?
Example split
Instead of one function that calculates damage and updates UI, make one that returns damage and a thin wrapper that applies UI updates. This separation improves testability.
Anti-pattern

A single function that handles game logic, I/O, and UI is hard to reuse and test. Break responsibilities into smaller functions.

Try this

Refactor one mixed function in your project: extract the pure calculation into a return-based function and keep the UI update separate.

screens.title: Starter code: Player Interaction System
screens.subtitle: A compact script that uses functions, checks, and an anonymous event handler

narration.text: This starter script demonstrates a small Player Interaction System that manages adding items to a simulated inventory and checks space before adding. It uses local functions for AddItemToInventory and CheckInventorySpace so their scope is limited to the script. The AddItemToInventory function simulates inserting an item into a table and returns true on success. CheckInventorySpace returns a boolean depending on available slots. The demo includes three scenarios that call these functions and an anonymous function connected to a part's Touched event to simulate giving an item to a player who touches a part. Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Player Interaction System
Starter Code Template
-- PlayerInteractionSystem
local playerInventory = {}

local function AddItemToInventory(itemName, quantity)
  print("Attempting to add " .. quantity .. "x " .. itemName .. " to inventory.")
  table.insert(playerInventory, {Name = itemName, Quantity = quantity})
  print(quantity .. "x " .. itemName .. " added successfully!")
  return true
end

local function CheckInventorySpace(itemCount)
  print("Checking inventory space for " .. itemCount .. " items...")
  if #playerInventory + itemCount <= 5 then
    print("Enough space available.")
    return true
  else
    print("Not enough space! Inventory full.")
    return false
  end
end

-- Demonstration
local itemsToGet = 2
if CheckInventorySpace(itemsToGet) then
  AddItemToInventory("Sword", itemsToGet)
end

-- Anonymous event simulation
local giveItemPart = Instance.new("Part")
giveItemPart.Name = "GiveItemPart"

giveItemPart.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
  local playerCharacter = otherPart.Parent
  local player = game.Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(playerCharacter)
  if player then
    if CheckInventorySpace(1) then
      AddItemToInventory("Health Potion", 1)
    end
  end
end)
This template simulates inventory logic and demonstrates event-driven invocation of helper functions. Replace prints with real inventory updates in a real project.
Exercise

Modify the CheckInventorySpace limit, then call AddItemToInventory several times and observe when adding fails. This helps you understand guard conditions.

Key Takeaway

Keep event handlers thin: validate inputs there and delegate logic to local functions that return clear results.

narration.text: Keep three quick reminders in mind as you write functions. First, name parameters clearly and keep functions short so their purpose is obvious. Third, validate event inputs inside callbacks and prefer local functions unless you intentionally design a global utility.
